title: Contract friction notes — rapid redlines
content:
Purpose: personal rapid-response scratchpad for contract negotiation. Designed to be copy/paste friendly during Slack or email pushback. Not authoritative — transmit to legal for final.

High-level posture:
- Preserve product access and predictable SLOs; avoid long tail operational obligations.
- Narrow indemnity triggers to gross negligence/wilful misconduct and clear carveouts for model outputs and third-party data where possible.
- Prefer limitations on liability tied to fees paid in trailing 12 months; push back on uncapped consequential damages.

Key friction clauses (priority ladder):
1) Liability cap & consequential damages
   - Ask: cap = greater of N months of fees or $X (use fee-based default). Resist per-occurrence unlimited caps.
   - Rapid snippet: "Supplier's aggregate liability shall not exceed the fees paid in the preceding 12 months. Neither party shall be liable for indirect, special, or consequential damages."
   - Escalation redline: if counterparty insists, propose carveouts: IP infringement (subject to indemnity), breach of confidentiality, or bodily injury only.

2) Indemnity (third-party claims)
   - Watch: broad IP indemnities that cover "any claim" including model outputs or Customer data.
   - Quick fallback: indemnify only for third-party claims alleging infringement of Supplier's underlying code/hosting (not model outputs or Customer prompt-derived content).
   - Talking point: we control runtime and model weights; model outputs are probabilistic and not warrantable. We can offer takedown/help with remediation.

3) Data residency & export controls
   - Flag: language requiring all data to remain in customer region or specific cloud. Operationally expensive for hosted service.
   - Fast counter: "Supplier will use commercially reasonable efforts to meet data residency, but Customer may need Dedicated/Private deployment for strict residency guarantees." Link to SKUs/Private offering.
   - If buyer demands: propose roadmap + SLA for dedicated capacity (escalate to sales/devops).

4) Audit rights & security assessments
   - Problem: unlimited on-site audits or full log access.
   - Tighten: accept third-party SOC2 summary, security questionnaire (e.g., shortform) and remote evidence. On-site only for material incidents with NDA and cost-shift.
   - Snippet: "Customer may request security artifacts; Supplier will provide SOC2 Type II report and cooperate reasonably. On-site audits subject to mutual NDA and cost recovery."

5) Termination & transition assistance
   - Avoid lengthy multi-month transition SLAs that create binding support obligations.
   - Offer: 30-day export window and API-based data export. Extended assistance as a paid professional services engagement.

6) Subprocessors & subprocessors
   - Keep list + notice. Avoid per-vendor approval. Approve vendor categories instead.
   - Snippet: "Supplier may engage subprocessors and will provide prior notice of material changes; Customer may object in good faith." 

7) Model output IP & ownership
   - Common ask: Customer owns all outputs. Risky when outputs are derivative of model weights or third-party content.
   - Middle ground: Customer has perpetual license to outputs for their use; Supplier retains model weights and operational IP. If customer needs assignment, escalate to legal/sales.
   - Snippet: "Supplier grants Customer a perpetual, worldwide, royalty-free license to use and exploit outputs generated from Customer prompts for Customer's internal and commercial purposes."

Practical negotiation tactics (rapid):
- Use the "three buckets" pitch: (1) Acceptable (confidentiality, KYC), (2) Negotiable with limited exposure (liability cap, indemnity carveouts), (3) Escalate to sales/legal (data residency, IP assignment, uncapped liability).
- Keep walkaway triggers short and numeric: e.g., "walkaway if unrestricted audit + uncapped liability + IP assignment requested".
- Offer swaps: if they want broader IP rights, ask for higher price or dedicated contract with clear SLA and insurance.

Prepared snippets (copy/paste):
- Confidentiality: "Confidential Information excludes aggregated or anonymized metrics and information independently developed by the receiving party."
- Liability cap: "Aggregate liability <= fees paid in preceding 12 months; excludes breach of confidentiality and willful misconduct."
- Indemnity (narrow): "Supplier will defend and indemnify Customer for third-party claims solely to the extent they allege Supplier's product code directly infringes a third party's patent, copyright, or trademark. Supplier will not indemnify for outputs produced by models."
- Data export: "On termination, Supplier will provide Customer with a machine-readable export of Customer data within 30 days; extended transition support available under a separate SOW."

Open questions / things to ask legal before finalizing:
- Is there a standard dollar default we should use for SMB deals vs enterprise? (ask sales ops)
- Suggested insurance threshold to offer in negotiations? (check with risk & insurance)
- Standard exception language for generative model hallucinations — do we have precedent language from AI policy team?

Personal TODOs:
- Pull latest SOC2 summary link and attach to Confluence page. (JIRA-CC-987)
- Draft a one‑pager on why model-output assignment is operationally problematic to share with GTM.
- Coordinate with Solutions Eng for quick Dedicated SKU price if customer demands strict residency.

Quick negotiation scripts (30s):
- If they push uncapped liability: "We can agree to a reasonable cap tied to fees or procurement spend. Full uncapped exposure isn't possible for a SaaS inference platform — the economic risk is too high."
- If they demand output assignment: "We can provide a perpetual license for outputs; assignment or transfer of underlying models requires a bespoke enterprise arrangement and additional compensation."

Last edits: keep this doc ephemeral. Port final snippets to Confluence/legal library if reused >2 times.

Notes to self: save three most-used snippets as templates in \confluence\legal-templates and add example PRs.
